content.text:
Our Child Who Keeps Cutting in Line

At the slide, the swing, or in line to play, your child shouts "Me first!" and squeezes right to the front of the line. Their eagerness gets ahead of them, and they just can't wait their turn.

But if one child keeps cutting in, no one else gets to enjoy it. Before you say "Wait!", it comes first to help your child feel for themselves why taking turns matters.

Curious about the taking turns storybook? Take a look at its lesson through pictures. Meet the key scenes of the tale too. Read it together with your child and talk about it. content.alt: 32. Turn by Turn, Me and You! - Why Does Taking Turns Matter?
content.text:
Why Does Taking Turns Matter?

Taking turns isn't just good manners; it's a basic part of living together in a community. A child who knows how to wait their turn builds both self-control and consideration for others.

In particular, the experience that "if we all wait a little, everyone has fun" teaches a child that rules are not a loss but a promise for everyone. This sense becomes a great strength at daycare, at school, and in relationships throughout life.

content.alt: 32. Turn by Turn, Me and You! - Toto and Kongi's Playground Story
content.text:
Toto and Kongi's Playground Story

In the story Turn by Turn, Me and You!, Toto keeps cutting in line. Then Kongi takes his hand and asks, "How would you feel if another friend kept cutting in front of you?"

Toto thinks hard and answers, "I think I'd feel upset too..." And when Kongi says, "If we go turn by turn, I get a turn and you get a turn and everyone gets to ride!", Toto's eyes sparkle.

content.alt: 32. Turn by Turn, Me and You! - The 3 Rules of Taking Turns You Learn with Tangobook
content.text:
The 3 Rules of Taking Turns You Learn with Tangobook

The heart of this story is three rules that are easy for a child to remember. One, line up! Two, wait for my turn! Three, when I'm done, it's the next friend's turn!

Tangobook's story repeats these rules like a refrain, helping your child naturally recall them at the playground. Just like Toto, who slides down joyfully after waiting, your child gets to feel the fun that comes after waiting.

content.alt: 32. Turn by Turn, Me and You! - Playing the Taking-Turns Game Together at Home
content.text:
Playing the Taking-Turns Game Together at Home

After reading the book, practice lining up by shouting "Turn by turn!" together at the playground. Whether it's the slide or the swing, turning taking turns into a game makes it naturally become second nature.

Then point it out: "Wasn't it even more fun to ride after waiting?" Helping your child imagine the other person's feelings and showing them the fun that comes after waiting makes them accept taking turns happily.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I teach taking turns?

A. Teach waiting your turn like a game, saying 'turn by turn, me and you.' When they experience the joy of their turn coming after waiting, children want to follow it on their own.

Q. What if my child can't wait their turn and throws a tantrum?

A. Help the waiting time not feel boring by counting or singing a song together. With a taking-turns storybook, they can naturally learn the joy that comes at the end of waiting.

Q. What do I do if there's a fight over turns at the playground?

A. First acknowledge the turn of the friend who arrived earlier, and confirm together the promise that yours comes next. Praising them when they wait well helps their patience grow.
